If the container has equal ears of area $a$ and the tips of its directed side vectors are in convex position, the sharp bound at $n=sk$ is $a/k^3$. Its equality conditions determine every side vector of the maximizing polygon. The proof uses the area enclosed by the normalized side directions. We compare the result with the area-normalized smallest-ear theorem of Gronchi and Longinetti and give consequences for unrestricted Heilbronn configurations with 13 and 15 points.
comments: 7 pages, 2 figures. Supplementary note, Lean formalization, and reproducibility files: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24497708

title: What Must LLM Agents Communicate? From Information Loss to Communication Failures
abstract: When evidence is distributed across LLM agents, a team may collectively possess all the information needed for a decision yet fail to use it effectively. What must agents communicate for accurate joint predictions, and when does interaction help? We study three requirements for effective communication: sufficiency of the information conveyed, selection of relevant evidence, and utilization of received information. Drawing on information theory and communication complexity, we develop a framework that combines theoretical benchmarks with controlled experiments and message-level analyses. We find that local probability reports can discard essential information, with theoretical information loss closely matching observed performance penalties. Query-first interaction improves predictions when relevant evidence depends on a private query, but compact one-shot representations can eliminate this advantage. Even when sufficient information is communicated, agents may fail to select or use it correctly. Together, these findings distinguish fundamental communication limits from failures in how LLM agents communicate and use information.

title: Differentiability of the shape function in the planar corner growth model
abstract: We prove that the shape function of planar directed last-passage percolation with general i.i.d.\ real-valued weights is differentiable on the open first quadrant, under a moment assumption of order $p''>4$ on the positive part of the weight and a nearly optimal order $p'>1$ on the negative part. Due to known results, only directions outside a percolation cone need be considered. The proof is a multiscale path-counting argument that uses the shape theorem, oriented percolation on a coarse-grained lattice, a simple change of measure in a finite region, and the van den Berg--Kesten inequality. Our Lean-formalized proof is an AI-assisted adaptation and improvement of the OpenAI proof of differentiability in planar first-passage percolation.
comments: 72 pages, 18 figures

title: The squared antipode of a twisted function algebra is locally unipotent
abstract: Let $G$ be a proalgebraic group over an algebraically closed field $k$ of characteristic zero, and let $F:{\rm Rep}(G)\to {\rm Vect}(k)$ be a dimension-preserving tensor functor, possibly nonsymmetric. We prove that a tensor automorphism $T$ of $F$ is locally unipotent if and only if its trace on $F(V)$ equals ${\rm dim} V$ for every $V\in {\rm Rep}(G)$. Applied to the Drinfeld element of a dual twisted function algebra $(\mathcal{O}(G)^J)^*$, this proves our conjecture from 2000 that the square of the antipode in $\mathcal{O}(G)^J$ is locally unipotent (arXiv:0002128). Without the trace assumption, we show that for any $V\in {\rm Rep}(G)$ the eigenvalues of $T$ on $F(V)$ determine, modulo roots of unity, its eigenvalues on $F(\mathbb{S}^νV)$ for every Schur functor $\mathbb{S}^ν$. The proof combines the Koszul identity, polynomial growth of symmetric powers, Fourier inversion, and congruences for Newton sums.
comments: 7 pages, latex; the main argument is due to ChatGPT 6 Astra

title: Singularities in global pluripotential theory
abstract: This book is an expanded version of the author's lecture notes at the Institute for Advanced Study in Mathematics (IASM) at Zhejiang University. We systematically develop the theory of plurisubharmonic singularities on compact Kähler manifolds and relate it to the non-Archimedean pluripotential theory and toric pluripotential theory.
comments: Pre-AI research monograph expanded from the author's lectures at Zhejiang university in 2024. All 849 statements in the book are formalised in Lean 4. Accepted by Springer's LNM

title: A Non-Commutative Binomial Theorem, Extensions, and Applications
abstract: This paper presents a matrix trace inequality analogous to the binomial theorem for reals: for Hermitian matrices $A$ and $B$, and a nonnegative even integer $k$ (and any nonnegative integer $k$ when $A, B$ are positive semi-definite), \[ \mathrm{tr}\bigl((A + B)^k\bigr) \le \sum_{\ell=0}^k \binom{k}{\ell} \mathrm{tr}\bigl(A^\ell B^{k-\ell}\bigr). \] The above natural inequality implies the classical Golden--Thompson inequality $\mathrm{tr}(e^{A + B}) \le \mathrm{tr}(e^A e^B)$. It also proves an extension, which can be used to show other new inequalities as well as give short proofs of inequalities such as the Schatten-$p$ two-point inequality for $p \ge 3$ and Hanner's inequality for $p \ge 3$. The main proof was discovered by Gemini Carbon within an agentic system.

title: PatternMiner: Automated Mathematical Discovery Through LLM-Guided Training and Interpretation of Small Models
abstract: There are several approaches to AI-driven mathematical discovery. One of these involves the use of large language models (LLMs) to resolve well-specified conjectures via text-based reasoning, while another uses narrow models and interpretability for more open-ended, human-in-the-loop exploration using object-based mathematical data. The latter is limited in its ability to move beyond simple empirical pattern detection while the former is not well-designed for direct, open-ended exploration of large mathematical datasets. In this paper we introduce PatternMiner, a system that combines these two paradigms. In PatternMiner, an LLM agent generates mathematical datasets based on an initial broad question, trains narrow machine learning models on them, uses interpretability techniques to extract patterns from these trained models, and uses these patterns to formulate conjectures. Once an initial conjecture has been formulated, PatternMiner instructs the agent to search for counterexamples using calls to mathematical software. If a set of counterexamples can be found, these are used as feedback for conjecture refinement or another round of training and interpretability. The conjecture progressively evolves through this iterative sequence with the agent allowed to try to prove it at any point. We describe the results of applying PatternMiner to five well-known positivity problems in algebraic combinatorics. PatternMiner proves several new theorems related to Schubert positivity and projection, a character-row evaluation formula, a restricted version of the Kazhdan--Lusztig combinatorial invariance conjecture, and Schur positivity for a family of immanant coefficients. We end by analyzing the most common routes to conjecture generation that are used by PatternMiner in our case studies as well as documenting the most common failure modes.
comments: 46 pages. Code and experiment records are available at https://github.com/uw-math-ai/PatternMiner. Comments welcome!

title: Degree-respecting labellings with ordered neighbour sums
abstract: In an exhaustive enumeration of hydrocarbons with only single bonds, carbon skeletons are generated as adjacency matrices and pruned by two rules: a vertex of larger degree receives a smaller label, and among vertices of equal degree, a vertex whose adjacency row is the larger binary integer receives a smaller label. The pruning is sound only if every skeleton admits a labelling obeying both rules. We prove that such a labelling exists for every finite simple graph, connected or not and with no bound on the degrees, and that the same holds when the weights $2^i$ of the labels $i$ are replaced by any strictly increasing real weights. The proof takes, among the labellings that order vertices by non-increasing degree, one minimising the sum over edges of the products of the endpoint weights.
comments: 7 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Lean 4 formalisation: https://github.com/uda-lab/degree-labeling

title: The $k$-disjoint paths problem for group-labelled graphs
abstract: A $Γ$-labelled graph is an oriented graph with edge labels in a group $Γ$. Fix a finite abelian group $Γ$ and a positive integer $k$. We give a polynomial-time algorithm that finds $k$ vertex-disjoint paths joining prescribed pairs with a prescribed gain on each path, or determines that none exist. The result previously appeared only in the author's 2009 PhD thesis. This proof uses a reduction to unbreakable graphs and recent structure theorems for graphs drawn on a surface, and was found with the help of AI.
comments: 37 pages, 3 figures

title: A Counterexample to Single-Control Null Controllability of Stochastic Heat Equations
abstract: We disprove the conjecture that a single localized drift control suffices for null controllability of stochastic parabolic equations with bounded adapted coefficients. On a bounded interval with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions, we construct a deterministic, nonnegative smooth noise coefficient supported at positive distance from the control interval. One fixed nonzero smooth initial state cannot be driven to zero almost surely at any positive time by any progressively measurable control with finite expected $L^2$ energy. The proof uses products of Brownian increments in the adjoint terminal data to keep the initial pairing bounded away from zero while the observation norm tends to zero. On the flat torus, the construction yields counterexamples in every Gevrey class of order $s>1$ whenever the complement of the control set contains an open ball. Thus Gevrey regularity above order one cannot replace analyticity as a general sufficient condition for null controllability.
comments: 4 pages; Lean 4 formalization available at https://github.com/guohaoji21/stochastic-heat-lean

title: Routing and Cache Retention for Multi-Turn LLM Inference: Theory and Implementation
abstract: Multi-turn AI agents execute iterative loops of large language model (LLM) inference and external tool calls, transforming cluster serving into a dynamic resource-allocation problem where routing and key-value (KV) cache retention jointly govern prefix reuse across inter-turn delays. We formulate a fluid approximation of this system and show that optimal admission, routing, and eviction are governed by endpoint-specific shadow prices for computation and memory together with session continuation values. Building on this structure, we propose an asymptotically optimal buffer-reserve policy that absorbs stochastic fluctuations using a vanishing share of capacity. To handle asynchronous arrivals, delayed load reports, and engine-local memory management in production clusters, we translate these principles into a practical controller named PARK, which pairs online projected subgradient price updates and one-turn migration lookahead with a local KV retention index ranked by expected reuse value per byte-epoch. In real GPU cluster experiments serving a 197-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model on multi-turn software-engineering agent benchmarks (SWE and Terminal-Bench), PARK outperforms all five load-balancing and prefix-aware baselines across contrasting traffic regimes. On 16 H200 GPUs, PARK raises output throughput by $24.2\%$ over the strongest baseline ($336.9\%$ over round robin) on turn-intensive SWE trajectories and by $40.0\%$ over the strongest baseline ($63.3\%$ over round robin) on generation-intensive Terminal-Bench trajectories. Controlled single-replica ablations show that our retention index alone cuts prior-prefix token loss from $13.26\%$ to $2.17\%$ and increases throughput by $36.7\%$ over least-recently-used (LRU) eviction, while 128-GPU scale-up experiments sustain 50,789 to 67,363 output tokens/s across 16~replicas with prefix cache hit rates of $91.3\%$ to $97.4\%$.

title: Territorial Conflict as a Cellular Automaton: Frozen Domains and Active Fronts in a Risk-Derived Local Rule
abstract: We formulate the attack and fortification rules of the game Risk as a synchronous cellular automaton on a graph, with battles resolved by exact dice odds. We prove, and verify in Lean, that for the default exchange ratio the rule has radius 6, or 5 for deterministic battles with a positive attack threshold, both attained; that its deterministic form is irreversible except at the highest attack thresholds without growth and with fortification absent or inactive; that without troop growth it freezes in finite time; and that the dynamics near an interface is locally determined. The coupling of the ownership field to a troop field separates frozen domains from active fronts: with a positive attack threshold, saturated domains cannot be conquered, while interfaces with heterogeneous troops keep fighting. In 14252 runs, with attractors classified operationally in Wolfram's scheme, raising the attack threshold takes the system from dominance by one faction to a frozen fragmented partition. The share of the largest faction drops between the same two threshold values at every size up to L=128, in a step about 0.5 wide under a continuous threshold (L=64-96), whereas the probability of complete consolidation is a size-dependent crossover governed by saturated minority domains. Long-period attractors combine spatially fixed local oscillators; apparent class-IV gliders are artefacts of index-ordered tie-breaking. Straight fronts stayed within two cells of their initial position for up to 500,000 steps, over which they are one-dimensional automata with non-recurrent, incompressible dynamics and positive Lyapunov speeds, constant for L>=48. Compared with mean-field and random-regular-graph controls, the lattice lengthens conflicts about twentyfold and clusters conquest: a cell next to a fresh conquest is about five times as likely as average to be conquered next, against 1.1-1.5 in the controls.
comments: 35 pages, 15 figures, 25 tables. Submitted to Complex Systems. Code, data and Lean formalisation: https://github.com/MaTeArNog/RiskAutomata

title: Real equiangular lines in dimensions 18-20 and sharp fixed-angle bounds
abstract: In collaboration with OpenAI's GPT-6, we prove that the maximum numbers of real equiangular lines in dimensions 18, 19, and 20 are $N(18)=57$, $N(19)=72$, and $N(20)=90$, respectively. We reduce the upper bounds to paired lattice points in sections of even unimodular lattices of rank twenty-four. Root-system estimates, exact certificates, and Golay-code arguments bound the sections. In the Leech lattice, generalized Hamming weights of a binary evaluation code give sharp bounds attained by nested sections. At prescribed cosine $1/q$, we also show that $N_{1/q}(d)=d+7$ for explicit intervals of consecutive dimensions for each odd $q\ge319$, and $N_{1/q}(d)=d+23$ on such intervals for each odd $q\ge5599$. Regular graphs in repeated Seidel blocks vary the cosine while preserving nullity, and a coherence bound proves optimality. Symmetric conference matrices give a further sharp family at quadratic irrational cosines.
comments: 71 pages. Verification code and certificates are available at https://github.com/Wideep886/Equiangular_Lines_Maxima
